artworks.title: The Fury of Athamas
artworks.description: This colossal white marble group, carved in Rome by the English Neoclassical sculptor John Flaxman for Frederick Hervey, 4th Earl of Bristol, depicts the climax of Learchus's brief and tragic life. Driven mad by the wrath of Hera, King Athamas seizes his elder son Learchus by the ankle and swings the child overhead to dash him against the rocks, while his wife Ino recoils with the infant Melicertes. The straining, helpless body of Learchus is the dramatic pivot of the composition, his outflung limbs embodying the horror of a father destroying his own son. Commissioned for Ickworth in Suffolk, where it remains in the National Trust collection, the piece took Flaxman more than three years and stands as one of the most ambitious sculptural treatments of the Athamas myth drawn from Ovid's Metamorphoses.

artworks.title: Athamas Killing the Son of Ino (Athamas tue le fils d'Ino)
artworks.description: An oil on canvas (92 × 63 cm) by the late-Baroque Bolognese painter Gaetano Gandolfi, now in the Molinari Pradelli collection at Marano di Castenaso, Italy. The painting isolates the murderous moment itself: the frenzied Athamas grips the small body of Learchus, mistaking his son for prey in his Hera-sent madness, the child's pale limbs lit against the dark turbulence of the scene. Painted at the very end of Gandolfi's career, it concentrates the whole catastrophe of the house of Athamas onto the single figure of the doomed boy, rendered with the dynamic chiaroscuro and emotional intensity characteristic of the Gandolfi workshop.

artworks.title: The Insane Athamas Killing Learchus, While Ino and Melicertes Jump into the Sea
artworks.description: An etching (plate 39 of an illustrated edition of Ovid's Metamorphoses, published in Amsterdam by Wilhelm Janson after designs by the Florentine printmaker Antonio Tempesta) held by the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (acc. 65.37.123). In a single compact scene the print stages the whole tragedy named in its title: the maddened Athamas lifts and strikes down the child Learchus in the foreground, while at the cliff's edge Ino leaps into the sea clutching the younger Melicertes. As a widely reproduced book illustration, the image helped fix the iconography of Learchus's death for early-modern European readers of Ovid.

artworks.title: Athamas Seized by the Furies (Atamante preso dalle Furie)
artworks.description: A Neoclassical painting by Arcangelo Michele Migliarini, preserved at the Accademia di San Luca in Rome. It shows King Athamas in the grip of the avenging Furies, the divine madness that turns him against his own family. The infant Learchus appears among the imperilled figures of the household alongside Ino and Melicertes, the young child rendered as the vulnerable victim at the center of the unfolding violence. Produced as an academic competition piece, the work exemplifies how the Athamas-and-Learchus episode served around 1800 as a vehicle for the heightened pathos and dramatic gesture prized in late-eighteenth- and early-nineteenth-century history painting.
